Patient Vignette: Mark

Mark is a 29-year-old single man who works as a salesperson for a regional office supply company. He presents for therapy at the urging of his supervisor, who has noticed a sharp decline in his performance over the past eight months. Mark is lean, with a nervous energy that makes him seem perpetually on the verge of standing up. He speaks in short, clipped sentences, his eyes often darting to the window.

The event that changed everything happened on a Tuesday afternoon in early spring. Mark was driving home from a client visit in a rural part of the county. The sky had been a strange, greenish-yellow for hours, but he didn't think much of it-the weather app had only warned of thunderstorms. Then the radio went silent. A moment later, his car began to shudder, not from the engine, but from the ground. He pulled over on a gravel road, thinking it was an earthquake. When he stepped out, he saw it: a massive, rotating wedge of cloud descending from the sky, less than a mile away. The sound was not a roar but a deep, physical pressure in his chest, like a bass note played directly on his organs.

He ran. Not toward shelter-there was none-but into a shallow ditch beside the road. He lay face down, arms over his head, as the world tore itself apart around him. He remembers the sensation of being lifted, just slightly, his feet leaving the ground for a second. He remembers the smell of wet earth and gasoline. When it was over, he stood up in a landscape that had been rearranged. A barn that had been across the field was simply gone. His car was peppered with dents from flying debris, but it still ran.

In the weeks that followed, Mark told himself he was fine. He had survived. He hadn't even been physically hurt. He returned to work the next Monday, shaking hands and smiling at clients. But inside, something had short-circuited. He began to experience a low-level hum of anxiety that never fully turned off. He stopped watching the weather forecast because the mere sight of a meteorologist on screen made his heart race. He started driving to client meetings only on clear days, and if the sky looked threatening, he would cancel, making excuses about a stomach bug or car trouble. His sales numbers have dropped by forty percent.

In session, Mark describes a specific, recurring memory that feels more real than the present moment. It is not the tornado itself, but the moment before-the green sky, the radio static, the silence of the birds. He will be sitting in a restaurant with a client, and a truck will rumble past, and suddenly he is back in that ditch. His hands tremble. He feels the gravel under his palms. He becomes irritable and short-tempered, snapping at waitstaff or his clients for no reason. He has stopped dating because he cannot explain why he needs to sleep with a flashlight on, or why he checks the barometric pressure on his phone every morning.

The most isolating part, he says, is the sense that he lives in a different world now. His colleagues joke about the weather. His friends ask why he never wants to go on a weekend trip to the lake. He cannot tell them that the sight of a dark cloud on the horizon feels like a personal threat, a predator that has found him once and is looking for him again. He spends his weekends in his apartment, blinds drawn, watching old sitcoms on low volume. He feels like he is waiting. He doesn't know what for, but he is certain it is coming.
